title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
content:
I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.

It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.

I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it. Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica

The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”

I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving my seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.

The shopping experience

Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”

title: Dig through an infested planet with your giant drill-city and try not to die while you do it in the roguelite city-builder CitaDrill
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Spin to win

You've heard of the drill that will pierce the heavens, so introducing: the drill that is attached to an entire city that will pierce the earth. That's the concept for CitaDrill, a roguelite city-builder where the city is encased in a big ole dome, a larger than life drill attached to its base that you dig through an infested planet. It's a lot, of course, but it's got some lush pixel art and a demo you can try out for yourself as part of this Steam Next Fest, too.

When you start things off, all you have is your humble drill, and a need to dig downwards. As you do so, drilling up different kinds of blocks nets you a range of resources, all dependent on the colour of the blocks you've crushed up. In typical city building fashion you use these to build up your domed city, with different fixtures providing various bonuses. Perhaps you add in a pressure valve to reduce a pressure buildup status, or you put up some power lines to get certain buildings and modules working. You may even decide to, uh, print a worker to get some jobs done.

Watch on YouTube

Of course what this is mostly all in service of is the drilling, but while you're doing that, you also have all sorts of nasty, giant creepy crawlies to worry about that want nothing more than to munch up your city. This then begets a tower defence element, whereby you need to attach various weaponry and defences to your drill-city in order to fend off incoming baddies (which, while slower paced and less screen encompassing, does have some bullet heaven vibes). There are some nasty looking bosses to fend off too, so you won't be starved of battles.

The game also has a whole cat thing going on? I think that's just for a touch of quirkiness, though it does do that thing where a real-world meme is referenced that I don't care for all that much, especially when it has so much style. Still, not offputting enough to not give it a go. Which, as a reminder, you can do! As it has a demo for you to try out on Steam right now ahead of its release before the end of the year.

title: Mass Effect Universe would have been a galactic Cold War with a John Wick-style N7 agent, claims creator who says he advised BioWare
author: Vikki Blake
content:
"And now we may never get to play it."

A content creator who claims to have served on a BioWare community council has shared alleged details about the cancelled next Mass Effect game, titled Mass Effect Universe.

In a lengthy Twitter/X post (thanks, PC Gamer), YouTuber Dantics claimed the cancelled game was set more than 600 years after the Reaper War.

He said he'd had access via his role on the "Mass Effect Council" and had seen firsthand what BioWare was developing, and provided feedback during development.

According to Dantics, the game would have centred on a "galactic Cold War" between three major factions, rather than another Reaper-style invasion. Humanity, the Krogan, the Batarians, and others would have allied, with the Council races forming their own alliance and the Geth emerging as a third superpower.

He also mentioned Geth-built megastructures, connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda, and a "shadowy adversary".

Players would have controlled a customisable N7 agent, which Dantics described as "a cross between John Wick and James Bond" rather than "a walking gun rack".

I can finally talk about Mass Effect Universe.

Since Bioware closed I can now reveal that I was part of the Mass Effect Council, saw what BioWare was building, and provided feedback during development.

• Set 600+ years after the Reaper War• You play as a customizable N7… pic.twitter.com/69b1HP1wm9

— Dantics (@DanticsOfficial) October 23, 2026

They would also have had experimental technology implanted, giving them the ability to hack and manipulate the environment, see through walls, identify systems, and remotely trigger hazards.

Missions would have been handcrafted, as in the original trilogy, but with "Hitman-style freedom" in how they were completed. Dantics also listed brutal close-range executions, squadmates who could clash with each other, romances that weren’t "sanitised", and Shepard’s legacy being preserved regardless of which ending players chose.

Squad member Liara would also have returned, only now as an "incredibly powerful Asari Matriarch".

"From what I saw, BioWare was making Mass Effect for us, the fans, not for people who don’t exist," Dantics wrote. "It looked incredible. And now we may never get to play it."

None of this has been confirmed. Neither BioWare nor EA has commented, and Dantics’s role on the council hasn’t been independently verified.

It follows the appearance of an internal trailer for Mass Effect Universe, which has since been confirmed as real, after BioWare’s closure and the cancellation of the game.

The EA job cuts, which took place only a few months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of the company, also hit developers at Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and other EA-owned studios. While such cuts were anticipated by experts given EA's new debt obligations, the news of BioWare's closure nonetheless drew out many messages of sympathy and anger from across the industry.

We said a sad farewell to BioWare earlier this week.

title: Epic Games further doubles down on gen-AI tools for Fortnite, Unreal Engine 6 and more: "Our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code"
author: Kaan Serin
content:
"We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

To no one's surprise, Epic Games has now confirmed that it's tripling down on its gen-AI push and will use the controversial tech on everything from Fortnite to the next iteration of its widely-used game development engine, Unreal Engine 6.

Speaking to This Week In Video Games, executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer confirmed that "we are definitely using AI to develop code and features for Unreal Engine," but that work will also be extended to the engine's next big numbered version. "Almost all development happening right now is being done in the dev streams attached to Fortnite, UEFN [Unreal Editor for Fortnite], and UE6."

When asked specifically if Epic is vibe-coding anything related to Unreal Engine, Wassmer put it plainly: "Yes, we are vibe-coding things. That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We're not 'one-shotting' the engine; we're iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes." Wassmer claimed the AI tools would help the company push out updates faster and with fewer bugs.

Epic seemingly isn't sweating over the divisive reaction to its gen-AI push, either - even as workers worry about job security, developers worry about plagiarism, and communities across the world worry about its environmental impact. Wassmer explained the company is "more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

"We don't think it's viable to take a halfway approach to AI in development," he added. "We think it's best to just be up front with what we're doing, share best practices with other developers, and make the best UE6 we can with the best tools available at any given time."

Earlier this month, Epic proudly admitted to vibe-coding the latest iteration of the Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to run slightly faster than Steam. "Prograaming is hard," the multi-billion dollar company explained at the time. "So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded the new Epic Games Launcher." Developers working on a troubled Disney and Marvel shooter were reportedly told to let gen-AI handle code and art production, too.

Epic CEO Tim Sweeney then started an online debate over Valve's AI policy that asks developers to disclose gen-AI use on their Steam pages. Sweeney argued that "forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mod they're helping organize is abhorrent." It's not surprising to see Epic dig its heels in further, then.

title: As No Man's Sky arrives on mobile, Hello Games celebrates with a spooky update for all that includes delivery missions and "seamless" interstellar travel
author: Matt Wales
content:
In space, everyone can hear you scream.

Today's the day iPhone and iPad owners finally get to boldly go into No Man's Sky's procedurally generated universe, adding two more devices to the game's already long list of compatible platforms. But developer Hello Games isn't stopping there. It's also launching a new update, Forsaken, for all players, bringing a bit of seasonal spookiness to the exploratory space sim.

With No Man's Sky's big tenth anniversary update now out in the wild and its associated limited-time expedition over, Hello Games is taking players to what it calls the "darker side of the universe" this Halloween. Here, we're told, enigmatic traders are gathering in search of strange samples - ranging from haunted tech to biological horrors - and it's up to players to step out in search of them. That means dives into No Man's Sky's creepier corners, including derelict hulks, abandoned freighters, and infested outposts.

In return for their labours, players can acquire new seasonally themed shipbuilding options - leaning into the "creepy and organic side of sleek". These include biomechanical corvette modules, new cockpits, and a new interior set "inspired by a distant galaxy". Additionally there are new weapon and space suit styles: the larva tank helmet and wriggling grub cannon multi-tool. Hello Games' pre-release press material is a bit vague on whether this is all limited time stuff - perhaps in the form of a new Expedition - but there's also mention of "new features and gameplay" that sounds a little more permanent.

For instance, there’s talk of new postal missions - which see players "becoming a delivery driver across the galaxy" - alongside UI tweaks, including a radial menu for weapon selection, a new minimal HUD mode, and "dozens" of accessibility additions. The studio has also added what it calls "seamless warping", meaning you can just lock onto the brightest star in the sky and travel straight there without visiting the galactic map.

So that's the Forsaken update, which is available today on Mac, PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Switch 1 & 2, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S, VR, and - as now - iPhone and iPad. No Man's Sky is said to work with iPhone 11 and above, as well as 3rd Generation iPad Air and above, with the first bit of the exploratory space sim available to try for free. Mobile players can expect custom touch controls, all 40+ previously released updates, and a svelte 4GB download size.

So there you go! Full patch notes for No Man's Sky's Forsaken update can be found on Hello Games' website. And if you're in the mood for a bit more related reading, Eurogamer recently spoke to the No Man's Sky players building utopia at the end of the universe - and it's a fascinating story.

title: Donald Glover is heading up a PUBG live action series for Netflix
author: Andy Chalk
content:
PUBG, the battle royale that lets you wear a frying pan on your ass to keep it from getting shot off, is being made into a live action series for Netflix.

Narrative isn't really PUBG's strong point, but this one might be interesting for one big reason: Donald Glover is set to write, direct, and executive produce the series, and will also star in it. Stephen Glover, Donald's brother and frequent collaborator, is also attached to the project as writer and executive producer.

Glover has won numerous awards over the years for writing, acting, and music (under his stage name Childish Gambino), to the point that "list of awards and nominations received by Donald Glover" has its own remarkably lengthy Wikipedia page. Highlights include two Primetime Emmy awards, two Golden Globes, five Grammy Awards, two Peabody Awards, and five Writers Guild of America Awards.

The upside of PUBG not having a strong pre-existing story like, say, Halo or Fallout is that it affords creators the opportunity to do their own thing, and as I said, that could be very interesting indeed with Glover at the helm. His 2018 music video for This Is America, built around themes of racism and gun violence in the US, was critically acclaimed and won multiple awards, but also attracted considerable controversy over its violent content. More recently, his Mr. & Mrs. Smith series on Amazon Prime, which premiered in 2024, drew 16 Primetime Emmy nominations for its first season, including "Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series" for Glover himself.

No other details about the upcoming PUBG show on Netflix were announced, but even so, I'm definitely curious about this one and looking forward to learning more.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

title: Havn HS 360 review
author: @pcgamer
content:
The Havn HS 360 only improves on the winning formula of the HS 420. It's a little smaller, and it's easier to build into, but it's not a whole lot cheaper. Still, it's undoubtedly one of the best-looking mid-tower cases in the biz.

For

  • Stunning looks
  • Spotless construction
  • Gorgeous side panels
  • Good airflow
  • Excellent cable management

Against

  • Long cable runs for fans
  • VGPU version is expensive and a little cluttered
  • No fans included

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

The Havn HS 360 is a familiar sight. More or less the same design as the company's first case, the HS 420, it's just a touch smaller. That's no bad thing; the HS 420 earned a 90% score from me due to its ability to hide most of the ugliness that comes with the usual pile of cables and connectors behind its retro futurist style facade. I feel just as positively about this slightly shrunken version too.

The HS 360 is available in two versions, with or without vertical GPU mounting; and two colours, black or white. I've here two cases for review, covering all the options, and I've decided to put them to the test with rival builds. Namely to get a feel for the process of building with the different GPU mounting solutions, but also satiate my longstanding desire to build yin and yang gaming PCs. Dark and light. AMD and Nvidia.

I had a really good time with the HS 360. Both times. It has a few limitations to be aware of, especially regarding fan size, but select the right parts and a build comes together very easily. Both of my builds have come out looking stunning, and while I'd like to take all the credit, the HS 360 made very light work of cable management and overall aesthetics.

I definitely have a favourite from my two PCs, and the reasons why are down to the HS 360. So let's talk about the case in greater detail.

Buy if...

✅ Your PC has pride of place on your desk: The HS 360 looks fantastic and importantly isn't as huge as the HS 420.

Don't buy if...

❌ You can't spare more of your budget for fans: There are no fans included with the HS 360, which makes its high price tag even higher for a complete build.

The Havn HS 360 only improves on the winning formula of the HS 420. It's a little smaller, and it's easier to build into, but it's not a whole lot cheaper. Still, it's undoubtedly one of the best-looking mid-tower cases in the biz.

The HS 360 introduces some key design changes over the HS 420. Common across both standard and VGPU models are some quality of life improvements: support for Back Connect motherboards, a tighter bend on the panoramic glass panel, and larger cutouts for jamming a screwdriver through to the screws on the PCIe expansion slots.

Havn seems to have paid close attention to some of the feedback from builders with the HS 360, and it's now possible to install or replace two rear fans without having to remove components that may be already installed inside the case; a small but constant frustration with the HS 420.

The VGPU model also receives a new magnetic 'Airflow Divider' intended to keep the hot air produced by the graphics card from recirculating around it, which can increase temps. This works in conjunction with another glass divider mounted to the tilted fan bracket included with the VGPU model. As you'll see, there's a lot more going on with the VGPU model, and as such, it costs $80 more.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The standard model is a more simple thing. That's how I like it. It includes a three-fan bracket at the bottom, though unlike the VGPU model, these are flat and pointed straight at the graphics card. It also has an integrated GPU support that neatly sits atop of the lower cable routing points. This is fairly adjustable and can be removed entirely if you prefer.

There are no fans included on the HS 360. You're required to source your own at added expense, but be warned, unlike the HS 420, which supports a mix of fan sizes, the HS 360 only supports those 120 mm in size. Even in the top, it's limited to a maximum radiator size of 360 mm. It's easy to see why once I'd built a PC inside here: even with such a radiator installed, there's only a small amount of clearance between the motherboard on one side and glass on the other.

At least you don't need to worry about a fan controller, as one of those is included in the case. It's neatly stored rearwards in the back of the chassis.

Dust filters, you've got two of 'em. One in the bottom for those three intake fans, and one in the lower position in the rear. Though technically the rear and top panels also have non-removeable filters to keep dust from gathering elsewhere.

The storage bays are surprisingly brilliant on the HS 360, and it's a shame I don't really have any use for them. There are two included. Each holds two 2.5-inch SSDs or one 3.5-inch HDD. A series of screws lets you break them down to the basic cage for a hard drive and back up to the neat, space-saving unit you see on the back. If you prefer, ditch both and mount three more 120 mm fans in their place. You could even fit an AIO here, providing it doesn't exceed a thickness of 58 mm.

Havn also notes limited support for an AIO at the bottom of the case, but it limits GPU slots and it's a terrible idea for pump longevity and noise. Just don't bother.

Other bits included in the box are some zip-ties and hook-and-loop fasteners (you'll be needing these), a couple of spare sliders for the cable grommets, a VESA mounting bracket (for tiny screens but also may be useful for reservoirs or 3D printed add-ons, etc.), and a few bags of labelled screws.

Installation

The HS 360 is smaller in every way to the HS 420—14.9% according to Havn—though for its slightly smaller size, it feels just as easy to build into.

The fans go in first, and without issue thanks to the removable brackets used throughout the HS 360. I was left wondering where best to run the cables at times, and turns out, I would later realise I got some of these a little wrong. Namely the ones in the bottom of the case, which have a slightly awkward run around the dust filter, but also the top rear fan. You will also need a couple of fan extension cables to reach all the way around to the hub or even the closest headers on the motherboard in my experience.

A power supply goes in easy; the HS 360 supports those up to 230 mm in length. You will need a traditional PSU here, as the sideways mounting position and stubby shroud on the HS 360 do nix any hopes of fitting a Corsair Shift unit. That applies to like a dozen people but unfortunately I am one of that dozen, as 60% or so of the PSUs I own are Shift models. I made do.

Cable management is simple and straightforward. Everything locks in place using the hook-and-loop fasteners, of which extra are included, and a good amount of the zip-ties, too. There are spots for extra fasteners but I just tie the cables down to the generous number of tie-down spots. Looks smart, doesn't take much effort, job's a good'un.

Now one reason for doing two builds here was to try out the VGPU bracket. I admit, I don't generally love VGPU mounting. It's usually more hassle than it's worth. But I've given it a go here on one of the machines, and, despite some extra tinkering required to remove the VGPU bracket to install the motherboard and then reinstall it again, it did go fairly well.

From my time with it, I still don't care much for VGPU. Sorry. It just clutters the build, leaves the GPU power cables hanging awkwardly in front of the RAM, and means you're having to think more about airflow with all those dividers. To me, it's just not worth the extra $80, and the simple, standard option for less cash is wholly more appealing.

Aesthetics

I shouldn't need to be too convincing here, as the HS 360 is one of the best-looking cases I've tested all year.

I'm a big fan of the rear panel. Its black accents should help with colour-matching components inside the case, too. You don't need expensive all-white parts here, even though I've (mostly) opted for it in the light build. Some black components should look just as excellent. Case in point, I ran out of white fans and used a couple of black fans in the rear and I dare say it looks pretty decent. You can be the judge of that, I suppose.

The glass panel has a slightly tighter curve than the HS 420, and is altogether stunning. The design of this case does a wonderful job of hiding the uglier parts of a PC—the cables, connectors, and clutter—out of sight.

Gallery

Image 1 of 57

Thermals

The going theory is you'll set up your fans to have the four in the lowest mounting points as intake, and the four in the highest as exhaust. That makes the most sense in this chimney-style design, but it does mean the most visible fans display their bad side (the side with the hub supports and stickers).

Reverse fans would be a good idea across the four lower intake fan positions in the HS 360. I've stuck with Havn's own fans for my own test builds, the H12. They look decent for a lack of any garish white stickers and matching tone, but I'd prefer a cleaner look if possible. Especially on the VGPU model, wherein those fans are tilted more into line of sight. Just feels like Havn is missing a trick here by not selling its own reverse option.

Airflow is pretty straightforward for the standard HS 360: hot air go up. It's a little more complicated on the VGPU model.

The new magnetic airflow divider and fixed divider on the fan mount essentially isolate the HS 360 VGPU into two zones: a cool zone and a hot zone.

The hot zone is anything above and around the side and rear of the graphics card; the cool zone is anything in front of and below the graphics card. Havn says this has two key benefits: one being the hot air can no longer leave the graphics card and be pulled back again by the intake fans on the front, and the other is the cool air from the lower fans cannot fly right past the graphics card's intake fans. Both should, in theory, reduce GPU temps by some margin.

Havn reports a reduction of around 1.4–1.8 °C in its own tests. My tests showed roughly a 1.4 °C reduction with the glass dividers compared to without. That's pretty bang-on, but nonetheless not enough to convince me to keep them.

I think the dividers clutter the case somewhat. Moreover, while Havn includes some colour-matching anti-vibration pads you can attach to the glass to rest it on top of the card and prevent the divider from sagging, the tubes from the liquid cooler can also lean on the glass, pushing it askew. I guess once again, it's just not for me.

As for CPU temps, the glass dividers didn't seem to make any difference whatsoever in my testing.

Value

The value proposition of the HS 360 is very different depending on whether you pick the standard or VGPU models.

The standard HS 360 costs $200. That's cheaper than the standard HS 420, which is currently at $250, but it wasn't always. The HS 420 has seen a couple of price increases in the US since its release in late 2024. It started out at $199, which was the price I reviewed it at. It later increased to $230 around April, 2025, and again to $250 around March, 2026.

The standard option has a lot going for it. It's one of the best-looking cases in the biz, and it feels every bit as premium as it looks. Compare the HS 360 to a lot of other would-be premium cases at similar price points, such as the Cooler Master HAF II 500, and the HS 360 is in a league of its own. But there is a price to pay somewhere; the quality of the HS 360 is countered by the complete lack of fans. That's something the Cooler Master has in swathes.

At least you're free to choose your fans here. You could cheap out on a couple packs of Arctic P12 Pro—$40 would get you either 10 standard fans or six RGB fans—or you could spend over $100 on a three packs of Havn's H12 to fill out the case entirely. When you start to consider $300 for the standard option, Cooler Master's HAF II 500 doesn't look so bad at $200. Nor does the excellent Corsair Air 5400 with three fans for $230.

The HS 360 is undoubtedly a premium option, but one I think you can argue for pretty easily. It really is fantastic in most ways, with some important quality of life upgrades, and it looks absolutely stunning.

I struggle more with the VGPU option. Being as objective as one can be with a predisposed dislike of vertical mounting, $280 just feels like a lot to ask with no fans included in the box. It is cheaper than the HS 420 VGPU at $330, but here's the asterisk. The HS 420 VGPU came out at $269 in the US. So, the HS 360 looks like a decent saving given today's price tags, but in the broader context, it doesn't feel quite so competitive.

Prices are much more consistent in the UK. The HS 360 is £170, which is a saving on the £200 asked for the HS 420 since its release; and the HS 360 VGPU is £240, comfortably under the HS 420 VGPU at £270.

Havn HS 360

The Havn HS 360 only improves on the winning formula of the HS 420. It's a little smaller, and it's easier to build into, but it's not a whole lot cheaper. Still, it's undoubtedly one of the best-looking mid-tower cases in the biz.

Jacob has been writing about PC hardware and technology for over eight years. He earned his first byline at PCGamesN before joining PC Gamer. He spends most of his time building PCs, running benchmarks, and trying his best to learn Linux.

title: Phantom Blade Zero dev says don't get the latest Nvidia drivers
author: James Bentley
content:
Phantom Blade Zero, the highly anticipated wuxia action RPG, is finally out in the world, and if you're planning on playing it on an Nvidia graphics card, maybe consider skipping the latest Nvidia driver update. Yes, that's the opposite of developer S-Game's pre-launch advice.

Today, the Phantom Blade Zero devs took to the Steam page with a post titled "Reason and Madness" recounting the history of the dev team, previous works, and how Phantom Blade Zero came to be. This is followed up with three announcements: a recommendation to download the 5 GB day one patch, encouragement to try the game on handhelds and lower-end/mid-range PCs, and, finally, advice not to use the latest Nvidia driver, 621.01.

It says, "Based on our testing, version 617.42 currently offers the best experience in Phantom Blade Zero. If you’ve installed a driver newer than 617.42, we recommend rolling back to 617.42 and choosing the clean installation option. Please stay on this version until Nvidia releases its next driver update, which we expect to arrive soon."

Game Ready Driver 621.01 launched on Wednesday, October 21, and, in addition to providing some bug fixes, it is intended to better support DLSS and RTX in games like Phantom Blade Zero, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and NBA 2K27.

The Phantom Blade Zero team does not elaborate on how the previous drivers are better than the current one, but the recommendation implies it's significant enough to negatively impact your experience.

Luckily, it's very easy to roll back Nvidia drivers in the Nvidia App. Simply boot it up, click on 'Drivers', then scroll down to whatever previous driver you want to roll back to, click the three dots on the side, and then click to install.

If you don't want to install the Nvidia app, you can roll back drivers by opening up the Device Manager, clicking on "Display Adapters", then right-clicking on your GPU, hitting "Properties", navigating to the "Driver" tab and then rolling back drivers there.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

We don't yet have a timeline on when Nvidia's next driver is due to be released, but S-Game seems to think it will be soon, so you can always hold out for that if you won't be playing the game in the near future.

James is a more recent PC gaming convert, often admiring graphics cards, cases, and motherboards from afar. It was not until 2019, after just finishing a degree in law and media, that they decided to throw out the last few years of education, build their PC, and start writing about gaming instead. In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

title: Cyberpunk 2 might include multiplayer quests after CD Projekt Red scrapped the feature in Cyberpunk 2077, according to new RPG job listing
author: Kaan Serin
content:
Two for two.

Cyberpunk 2 might try to revive Cyberpunk 2077's online ambitions, as a new CD Projekt Red job listing is looking for someone familiar with "multiplayer network architecture."

As spotted by Cheap Happens, the role-playing powerhouse is currently looking to hire a lead quest programmer for its upcoming open-world sequel. Buried away at the bottom of the job listing, under the "Nice To Haves" section, the studio asks for an "understanding of multiplayer network architecture and client-server synchronization for game state/ quests."

The multiplayer mention is by no means confirmation that Cyberpunk 2 - or whatever it ends up being called - will have co-op and other online modes, but it's definitely something CD Projekt Red is looking into. And it certainly makes sense, too.

Once upon a time, Cyberpunk 2077 was intended to receive a multiplayer portion sometime after its initial launch. Of course, at the time, the shaky state of the game's development meant that was no longer feasible and CD Projekt Red instead said multiplayer would come as its own "triple-A release." Eventually, the famed studio realised it simply had to focus on ensuring the base game was stable enough on its own, and shelved those online ambitions.

A few years back, Cyberpunk 2077's senior quest designer, Philipp Weber, told Eurogamer the company was "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day" by "building an online technology that can be seamlessly integrated into development of our future games."

More recently, in 2024, CD Projekt CEO Adam Badowski said the team were "considering" multiplayer elements for the Cyberpunk sequel back when the game was still in its early concept phases.

We don't know much else about the neon-drenched follow-up, but CDPR has been keeping series fans full and fed with continual updates to Cyberpunk 2077. Earlier this week, the game got an update celebrating the debut of Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2 on Netflix - everything from dual-wielding to cross-platform mods were added to the six-year-old game.

title: An Anxious Season for Muslims in Texas
author: @NewYorker
content:
Mohamed Hussein, a thirty-eight-year-old manager at a health-care company in Houston, is a lifelong conservative, describing himself as a proponent of small government who often votes Republican. He moved from Cairo to Texas as a young child, and professes “tremendous faith in America.” He is also a practicing Muslim who prays daily. In June, he went to the Republican Party of Texas State Convention, in downtown Houston, joining his father, Tarek, who was serving as a delegate.

Tarek Hussein, a physical therapist, founded the local chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil-liberties organization. With thousands of people assembled in the Houston convention center, Party members made several attempts to oust Tarek and another Muslim delegate, owing to their ties with CAIR, which Governor Greg Abbott has designated as a foreign terrorist organization. At one point, the G.O.P. chair told Tarek and the other delegate to leave the caucus. “There is a Democrat convention happening in a couple of weeks,” he said from the stage. “Join them.”

Mohamed Hussein told me that he was shocked by the hostility. At the convention, the Party approved a resolution that called on the legislature to declare Sharia a “seditious, subversive competing enemy.” Sharia is a form of guidance about how Muslims should live and worship, akin to the messages of the Ten Commandments. Yet, for two decades, many G.O.P. critics have conflated it with political extremism and terrorism carried out in the name of Islam. The resolution said that advocating for Sharia should be considered a crime, with punishments that include the stripping of U.S. citizenship and deportation. Hussein recalled, “When I read this, I’m thinking, Seditious? People to be denaturalized and deported? This is utter madness.” He added, “This is the party in power adopting this resolution with the intention of leveraging the state against a community.”

Hussein decided to remain at the convention. “I don’t know of any other solution than dialogue,” he said. On the final day, he attended a session with the Judeo-Christian Caucus, reasoning that, if Christians and Jews could come together, surely the attendees would be open to Muslim voices, too. But the moderator, a former Southern Baptist minister named Rick Scarborough, warned the attendees that they would encounter Muslims who only pretended to be accommodating. “I’ll guarantee, if they get power, they’ll cut your head off as believers of Christ,” Scarborough reportedly said.

Hussein spoke up several times. “I felt I had to preface it by apologizing to people,” he recalled, “because my intention was not to impose myself on the session, but I felt compelled to tell them that you have heard a lot of lies.” He talked with Scarborough afterward: “I asked him rhetorically, not expecting his response, ‘What do you want us to do? You want us to leave?’ In a heartbeat, he said, ‘Yes.’ ” Hussein retreated to an empty seat where he could be alone, and he wept.

The targeting of Muslims by politicians is not a new phenomenon in the United States. The attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon spawned a wave of anti-Muslim harassment and hate crimes. Donald Trump, who falsely claimed for years that Barack Obama was a Muslim, first tried to restrict immigration from majority Muslim countries nearly a decade ago. But, in his second term, he has led a groundswell of unsupported claims about an insidious Islamic presence in the country. Nearly seventy representatives have joined the Sharia-Free America Caucus, in the U.S. House of Representatives. One member, the Georgia Republican Andrew Clyde, posted on X, “No more Islamic immigration. Denaturalize, deport, repeat.”

Two weeks ago, federal agents raided the home of Ilhan Omar, a Muslim member of Congress from Minnesota whom Trump has repeatedly vilified, reportedly seizing notebooks, her mobile phone, and her passport. The goal, according to the Wall Street Journal, is to find evidence to denaturalize Omar, a Somali refugee who arrived in the United States at age twelve, and deport her. Trump has called the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, a “jihadist lunatic.”

Nowhere, it seems, has the vilification been more widespread than in Texas. Ted Cruz, the G.O.P. senator who has said that he wants to be President, told the crowd at this year’s national Republican midterm gathering in Dallas that “communists and Islamists” are “coming together and sweeping over the Democrat Party . . . . They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.” Earlier this year, Bo French, the Republican nominee for railroad commissioner (a position that actually oversees the regulation of oil and gas, not railroads), posted on social media, “I know I won’t rest until every muslim is gone.” Governor Abbott, a Republican who is running for a fourth term, designated CAIR a foreign terrorist organization only nine days after launching his reëlection bid. (CAIR called the move a publicity stunt with “no basis in fact or law,” and filed a lawsuit, which is ongoing.)

These attacks have prompted fresh efforts to mobilize Muslim voters in Texas. Although the group likely comprises less than two per cent of the state’s population, they could make a difference in this year’s unusually close contests for Senate, governor, and multiple congressional seats. Ahmad Siddiqi, who has served as the imam at the Kingwood Islamic Center, in the northeast Houston suburbs, since 2008, told me, “I think we were afraid in the beginning, because we would get the yelling, the screaming, and all of these things. But many of us have grown out of that phase. Now we want to stand our ground.”

On a Friday in late September, Siddiqi welcomed Imran Ghani, the director of the local chapter of CAIR—the one that Tarek Hussein founded—to address the congregation about the need for Muslim citizens to vote in November. The visit was arranged by Salam Arif, a local anesthesiologist, who said that it has been difficult to inspire his fellow-Muslims. “The perception of most of the people is: ‘Red state, my vote doesn’t count,’ ” he told me.

Ghani, who is thirty-seven and was raised mostly in Houston, had been on the job for around two months when Abbott designated CAIR as a foreign terrorist organization. “What did I just sign up for?” Ghani recalled thinking. “But very quickly I realized that this is a path of all of the great civil-rights organizations in American history. Whenever a civil-rights organization is effective, it will be targeted by certain members of the political establishment.”

At the Kingwood event, as more than two hundred men and women filed into their separate prayer halls, Ghani drew on several verses in Al-Hujurat, the forty-ninth chapter of the Quran, widely interpreted as a directive for the ethical treatment of one another and a call for Muslim unity. He said that a lack of political power has made the community an easy target. He reminded his listeners of the right to religious freedom under the Constitution, and urged them to be “openly Muslim” at a time “when there is all sorts of hatred being spewed by the political élite and our children are being attacked in schools.” And he directed the attendees to the volunteer voting registrars seated at tables in the mosque.

Afterward, Mir Ali Sadat, an internal-medicine doctor, made his way to a table to confirm that he was registered. “We have to vote,” he told me as he filled out a form. “We have to make a society where everyone respects everyone, regardless of their religion, their language, their looks, their skin, their gender.”

Jida Nabulsi is the Texas director of Emgage, a nonprofit founded twenty years ago to propel civic engagement in the Islamic community. When we met, she was standing in the blinding sun in an elementary-school parking lot in the Houston suburb of Cypress, alongside nine young staffers as they prepared to knock on hundreds of doors. Nabulsi said that the group was trying to motivate people “who are unregistered or haven’t been involved at all.” In addition to canvassing, Emgage conducts sessions in mosques and other locations that focus on the rudiments of voting. Nabulsi told me that a right-wing, anti-Muslim group had recently put up a post calling her a “Sharia operative.” In her view, the term “Islamophobia” isn’t adequate for such attacks; she prefers the more plainspoken phrase “anti-Muslim hate.”

One of the door-knockers, Abdullah Younes, a seventeen-year-old university student, allowed me to tag along as he made his rounds. He drove his black pickup truck through the exit gate of an upscale subdivision and parked on a deserted street. The work, which he has been doing since July after being recruited by a relative, can feel thankless. Guided by a canvassing app that helps Emgage workers identify likely Muslim households, he was ten houses into his route and starting to sweat through his shirt before anyone opened the door. One woman waved him away. At homes where there was no answer, he left behind a flyer that read “The polls are calling. Will you answer?”

Abdullah Antepli, a Turkish-born imam and scholar who is the president of Houston’s nonsectarian Rothko Chapel, believes that the anti-Islam rhetoric will continue, not only because it attracts votes for Republicans but also because, in his view, the response from Muslims is too weak and disjointed. Many Muslims, Antepli told me, “realize the American dream individually, but that individual success doesn’t translate into a collective civic response.” One reason, he said, is “the lack of connecting tissues between various racial and ethnic Muslim communities,” which include, among other groups, recent arrivals from “socioeconomically, politically, and historically very disconnected and fragmented parts of the world.” This lack of cohesion is evident, too, in Houston’s mosques, where, he said, many who attend prayer services “come five minutes before” and leave two minutes after the services have ended.

The day after I accompanied the Emgage canvassers, more than a dozen candidates for Congress, state legislature, and local office showed up at the Clear Lake Islamic Center, southeast of Houston, to make their pitches and take questions. Republicans were invited; none appeared. The event was part of a new monthly series led by Mohammed Nasrullah, a former Boeing project manager who once served as the chairman of CAIR-Houston’s board. He is pressing Muslim citizens to vote, in particular in local races, where a few thousand votes can be the difference. “What I notice,” he said, “is every four years they wake up and vote for President, and then they go back to sleep.”

A significant motivator this year is a revised K-12 curriculum, which was approved in September by the Republican-controlled State Board of Education and which casts Muslims in negative terms. In one lesson, students will be asked to explain early Islam in terms of the Prophet Muhammad’s “brutal military campaigns against Jewish and Christian tribes, the normalization and regulation of slavery, and the taking of female captives as harem slaves.” In another, they will have to describe “the teachings of jihad and how these teachings led to the expansion of Islam and the conquest of Christian lands.”

Dana Van De Walker, who is a professor and administrator at a community college in the northern Houston suburbs and a candidate for the State Board of Education, was campaigning at a mosque for the second time in forty-eight hours. Flipping just a few of the fifteen seats on the board, she told me, would give Democrats a majority and a chance to overturn the curriculum vote. “The thing that really pisses me off as a teacher,” she said, “is that we’re spending so much time talking about Islamophobia that we can’t talk about how we’re forty-fourth in the nation in eighth-grade English language-arts/literacy scores.”

As Rabeea Sultan Collier, a district-court judge who is running for reëlection, told the Clear Lake audience, the solution is as simple as it is urgent: “This last year, we have been under attack in a way that we’ve never seen before. So we want you to come out in numbers like they’ve never seen before.” ♦
